sysd-scale-001.title: Distributed transactions: one commit across many databases
sysd-scale-001.text: One database can make a transaction all-or-nothing on its own. Spread that transaction over several databases and nobody owns the promise anymore. A distributed transaction is a transaction that runs across multiple nodes in a network, depending on where the data lives. It must still be atomic: it completes in its entirety or not at all, so all nodes commit or all abort and the whole transaction rolls back. The system has to coordinate that commit or rollback as one unit. Isolation is the hard property, because global serializability can be violated even if each database is serializable. The common algorithm for completing one correctly is the subject of {{ref:sysd-scale-002}}. It suits updates that commit within milliseconds to a couple of minutes. Booking a flight, a rental car and a hotel is too slow for it, since it would lock resources for as long as a day. Such long-lived transactions use undo steps instead; see {{ref:sysd-scale-110}}.

sysd-scale-002.title: Two-phase commit: asking everyone to vote before committing
sysd-scale-002.text:
Several databases must all agree to commit a transaction, or none of them may. Two-phase commit is the distributed algorithm that makes every participant agree on whether to commit or abort. One node acts as the coordinator, and the protocol runs in two phases.

In the voting phase, the coordinator asks all participants to commit. Each one runs the transaction to the commit point and writes undo and redo log entries. Then it votes Yes or No, and the coordinator collects the votes. In the commit phase, if every vote was Yes, the coordinator sends commit. Each participant completes the operation, releases its locks and resources, and acknowledges. If any participant votes No, or the coordinator's timeout expires, the coordinator sends rollback instead, and each participant undoes the transaction from its undo log.

The protocol assumes every node has stable storage with a write-ahead log that survives a crash, so recovery can finish after a failure. Those log records are slow to generate.

The weakness is blocking. A participant that has voted Yes must wait for commit or rollback, so if the coordinator fails permanently, some participants never resolve their transactions. It also cannot dependably recover when the coordinator and a participant both fail in the commit phase, because the failed participant may already have committed. It works through many temporary failures, but rare cases need manual intervention. It is not two-phase locking, which is a concurrency control protocol. In architectures built from many small independent services it is regarded as an anti-pattern, because it ties all participants more tightly together.

sysd-scale-014.title: Lamport timestamps: ordering events without a shared clock
sysd-scale-014.text:
Two machines never agree exactly on what time it is, so a timestamp from one clock cannot settle which event came first. A Lamport timestamp is a simple logical clock algorithm for ordering events anyway. Each process keeps a numeric counter that only has meaning relative to the messages moving between processes. It increments the counter before each local event and attaches it to every message it sends. On receiving a message, it sets its counter to the greater of its own value and the message's, then adds 1.

The guarantee runs one way. If event a happened before event b, the counter for a is smaller than for b, but a smaller counter does not prove the order. Events in processes that never exchange messages are concurrent and cannot be ordered. Breaking ties with something like the process ID gives a total order, though an artificial one that implies no causality. The two-way guarantee needs other techniques; see {{ref:sysd-scale-024}}.

sysd-scale-006.title: Heartbeats: how a cluster notices a dead machine
sysd-scale-006.text:
A crashed machine does not announce itself. The other machines notice only because something they expected stopped arriving. Heartbeats are periodic signals that let a distributed system monitor the health and status of its components. In the push style, a node signals another node or a monitor at a regular interval, and silence beyond a set interval means failure. It is simple, but network congestion can cause false positives. In the pull style, a central monitor asks nodes for status, which reduces traffic but may slow detection.

The interval is a trade-off: a short one costs overhead, while a long one makes everything wait. A false alarm that triggers failover can be highly undesirable, so the heartbeat transport must be reliable, often over more than one path. A cluster manager can track each node as Down, Init or Alive, and an Alive node that misses its acknowledgement timeout moves to Down. Protocols that make a group of machines agree also use heartbeats to maintain a quorum, a majority of nodes able to decide; see {{ref:sysd-scale-015}}.

sysd-scale-112.title: Happened-before: which events could have caused which
sysd-scale-112.text: Not every pair of events in a distributed system can be put in order. The happened-before relation orders events by their potential causal relationship in a concurrent system, especially an asynchronous distributed one. Within one process, events follow the order they occurred in, and a message send precedes its receive. Events in processes that exchange no messages, directly or through third parties, are concurrent: neither came before the other. Processes cannot know the relation unless they use a logical clock, such as a Lamport clock or the one in {{ref:sysd-scale-024}}. If processes may behave arbitrarily, it cannot be detected, because they can forge the metadata.

sysd-scale-024.title: Vector clocks: a counter per process to detect causality
sysd-scale-024.text:
A single counter per process cannot tell an ordered pair of events from a concurrent one. A vector clock can. It is a data structure that determines the partial ordering of events in a distributed system and detects causality violations. For n processes it is an array of n logical clocks, one per process, and messages carry the sender's clock state, as in {{ref:sysd-scale-014}}.

A process increments its own entry on an internal event or a send, and sends a copy of its vector with each message. On receipt it increments its own entry and takes the element-wise maximum with the received vector. One vector is less than another when every component is at most the other's and at least one is strictly smaller. If x happened before y, the vector for x is less than the vector for y. Lamport's 1978 clocks were scalars, and vector clocks generalize them. They reliably detect causality when processes only crash; when processes behave arbitrarily or maliciously, detection is fundamentally impossible. Cassandra uses them to ignore outdated state.

sysd-scale-003.title: Two-phase commit variants that send fewer messages
sysd-scale-003.text: Plain two-phase commit is chatty, and its log writes are slow. Its variants keep its guarantees while cutting messages, log writes or completion time. In one common architecture each participant talks to a nearby transaction manager, and the managers run the protocol among themselves, with no central component. Presumed abort and presumed commit assume a default outcome so messages and log writes can be skipped, at the cost of extra work during recovery. Tree two-phase commit puts the coordinator at the root of a tree of participants. Dynamic two-phase commit has no predetermined coordinator: Yes votes race up the tree, and the node where they meet takes charge.

sysd-scale-008.title: Consensus: getting machines to agree despite failures
sysd-scale-008.text:
Getting a group of machines to agree on one value sounds easy until some of them fail. That is the consensus problem: a number of processes, some of which may fail, must agree on a single data value. The processes put forward candidate values, communicate with one another, and settle on one, even though some may be faulty or unreliable. The payoff is practical. Consensus is used to agree on which transactions to commit to a database and in what order, and it underlies the techniques in {{ref:sysd-scale-020}} and {{ref:sysd-scale-113}}.

The obvious idea is to take the majority value, which needs at least one more than half of the votes. But faulty processes may skew the outcome, so that agreement is not reached or is reached wrongly. A real protocol must do better. The output must be the input of some process, since a protocol that always outputs 1 would be useless, and a process decides only once, irrevocably. With halting failures, a protocol must give three guarantees. Termination means every correct process eventually decides. Agreement means all correct processes decide the same value. Validity means that if all correct processes propose v, they decide v. A protocol that does this among n processes of which at most t fail is called t-resilient. Protocols are compared by running time in rounds of message exchange and by message complexity.

The best-known protocols, described in {{ref:sysd-scale-015}} and {{ref:sysd-scale-021}}, are used pervasively in distributed and cloud systems. They depend on an elected leader to make progress and tolerate only crashes, not arbitrary or malicious behavior.

sysd-scale-007.title: Distributed locks: only one worker at a time
sysd-scale-007.text:
When many machines share a job, something must make sure only one of them runs it. A distributed lock is a mechanism that ensures mutual exclusion across a distributed system. It lets only one node become the leader at a time and makes a scheduled task run on a single worker, which prevents duplicate execution. It also lets one process at a time use a shared resource such as a file system or network socket. Locks bring deadlock, where processes each hold a lock another needs; the lock manager reports it to one request, and that process must resolve it.

The Google SRE book advises renewable leases with timeouts rather than indefinite locks, because a lease stops a crashed process from holding a lock forever. Chubby keeps lock information in small files in a replicated database on a fault-tolerant log run by the protocol in {{ref:sysd-scale-015}}. ZooKeeper and Redis, via the Redlock algorithm, can also provide locks. A lock is a low-level primitive to use with care; the SRE book says most applications should use a higher-level system instead.

sysd-scale-020.title: State machine replication: identical copies from ordered commands
sysd-scale-020.text:
Any deterministic program can be made a highly available replicated service by turning it into a replicated state machine. State machine replication is the technique for converting an algorithm into a fault-tolerant, distributed implementation. Its foundation is consensus: the copies agree on a global order for the operations, and each executes them in that order. Ad-hoc techniques may leave important failure cases unresolved, while the principled approach proposed by Lamport and others handles all cases safely.

In a leader-based design, each client request is a command. The leader appends it to its log and applies it to its own state machine once it is committed, as described in {{ref:sysd-scale-021}}. In the older family of protocols described in {{ref:sysd-scale-015}}, a continuous stream of agreed values acts as commands. Replicated state machines are the building block of data and configuration storage, locking and leader election. Because not every member of the group is in each quorum, a member may need to synchronize state from peers, for example with a sliding-window protocol.

sysd-scale-012.title: Single-value and multi-valued consensus
sysd-scale-012.text: Do the machines agree once, or over and over? Single-value consensus agrees on one value, while multi-valued consensus agrees on a series of values over time. Single-value protocols, described in {{ref:sysd-scale-015}}, settle on one value, which can encode metadata such as a transaction committed to a database. Binary consensus restricts the value to a single binary digit, 0 or 1; it is a building block for general protocols, especially asynchronous ones. Multi-valued protocols, covered in {{ref:sysd-scale-017}} and {{ref:sysd-scale-021}}, agree on a series of values forming a growing history. Running single-value consensus repeatedly works, but dedicated protocols are more efficient.

sysd-scale-011.title: Synchronous and asynchronous systems: do messages move in rounds?
sysd-scale-011.text: Does a system move in lockstep rounds, or does each message arrive whenever it arrives? In a synchronous system all communication proceeds in rounds. A process sends all the messages it needs in a round and receives all those from the others, so no message influences others sent in the same round. In an asynchronous system, messages have no such round structure. Real-world communication is often inherently asynchronous, but synchronous systems are easier to model. Consensus can be studied in either model. In a fully asynchronous system with a crash failure, the FLP result, described in {{ref:sysd-scale-010}}, rules out a deterministic algorithm.

sysd-scale-004.title: Three-phase commit: removing two-phase commit's blocking
sysd-scale-004.text:
Two-phase commit can leave participants stuck, waiting for a coordinator that never returns. Three-phase commit is a distributed algorithm that makes all nodes agree to commit or abort a transaction without that indefinite blocking. It splits the commit phase of two-phase commit in two. After the vote, the coordinator issues a pre-commit message that every participant must acknowledge, and only then does it send the final commit.

The extra step removes the ambiguity. The coordinator sends doCommit only after all participants have acknowledged they are prepared, so no participant can have committed before all know the decision. Every phase can time out, so there are no indefinite waits. If the coordinator fails before sending preCommit, the participants agree the operation was aborted. A recovery coordinator queries the participants: if some are already in the commit phase it drives the protocol to commit, and if none received PrepareToCommit it safely aborts.

The price is an assumption. The protocol needs bounded network delay and bounded node response times. With unbounded delays and process pauses it cannot guarantee atomicity, and it needs at least three round trips, which adds latency. In Skeen's original protocol a quorum can be connected yet unable to make progress; Keidar and Dolev's E3PC refines it so a quorum always can.

sysd-scale-114.title: The Two Generals' Problem: why certainty is impossible
sysd-scale-114.text:
Two generals must attack at the same time, or the lone attacker dies. They can only communicate by messengers sent through enemy territory, and any messenger may be captured. This thought experiment, the Two Generals' Problem, illustrates the pitfalls of coordinating an action over an unreliable communication link. An acknowledgement can be lost as easily as the original message, so no number of confirmations leaves each general sure the other agreed. A potentially infinite series of messages would be needed.

It was the first computer communication problem proven unsolvable: for any deterministic protocol, the sender of the last delivered message cannot tell whether it arrived. That is why TCP cannot guarantee state consistency between its endpoints. In practice, engineers accept the uncertainty and reduce it to an acceptable degree, for example by sending many messengers. No rule can be certain to prevent one general attacking without the other.

sysd-scale-009.title: Crash and Byzantine failures: stopping versus lying
sysd-scale-009.text:
A crashed machine at least has the decency to go quiet. A process can fail in two broad ways. It can crash, which means it abruptly stops and never resumes. Or it can fail in a Byzantine way, where no conditions are imposed on its behavior. A Byzantine process may come from a malicious adversary, may send contradictory or conflicting data to other processes, or may sleep and then resume after a lengthy delay.

Byzantine failures are far more disruptive than crashes, so a protocol that tolerates them must be resilient to every possible error. Agreement among such processes also needs a stronger integrity rule: if a correct process decides v, then some correct process must have proposed v. The numbers are unforgiving. With n processors of which f are Byzantine, no algorithm solves consensus for n ≤ 3f when messages are oral. When messages are written, meaning signed, protocols exist that tolerate n = f + 1. Digital signatures let each receiver learn who originally created a message.

The protocols in {{ref:sysd-scale-015}} and {{ref:sysd-scale-021}} tolerate only crashes. PBFT is a Byzantine-tolerant protocol, listed with the threshold n > 3f.

sysd-scale-113.title: Atomic broadcast: everyone sees the same messages in the same order
sysd-scale-113.text:
Send the same messages to every replica in the same order and the replicas stay in step. Atomic broadcast, or total order broadcast, is a broadcast in which all correct processes receive the same set of messages in the same order. It is atomic because it either completes correctly at all participants or all abort without side effects. Total order is not FIFO or causal order: every participant simply receives messages in the same order, whatever the order of sending.

Without failures it is easy: everyone follows a leader that decides the order. It is hard when computers fail, for example when the leader fails at the wrong time. With crash failures it is equivalent to consensus. Consensus reduces to it by proposing a value as a broadcast and deciding the first message received, and the reverse runs consensus on each next message. So the FLP result, described in {{ref:sysd-scale-010}}, applies to it too, though in practice it can be implemented by assuming less than FLP does about timings.

sysd-scale-111.title: ZooKeeper: a shared coordination service for cloud applications
sysd-scale-111.text:
ZooKeeper was the first open-source consensus system to gain traction, says the Google SRE book, because it was easy to use even for applications not designed for consensus. Apache ZooKeeper is an open-source server for highly reliable distributed coordination of cloud applications. It offers a hierarchical key-value store that serves as a configuration service, synchronization service and naming registry. Data lives in a tree of nodes, like a file system, that clients read and write to share configuration.

The service is replicated over an ensemble of servers, each holding the whole data tree in memory plus a transaction log and snapshots on disk. Clients keep a TCP connection for requests, heartbeats and watch events. It can be viewed as an atomic broadcast system in which updates are totally ordered, and the ZooKeeper Atomic Broadcast (ZAB) protocol is its core. Typical uses are naming, configuration management, data synchronization, leader election and notification, as well as barriers and distributed locks. It is fast for read-dominant workloads, scales by adding nodes, and was modeled after Google's Chubby lock service.

sysd-scale-010.title: The FLP impossibility result: a limit on agreement
sysd-scale-010.text: In 1985, three researchers proved something that sounds like a ban on distributed computing. Fischer, Lynch and Paterson showed that in a fully asynchronous message-passing system where even one process may crash, no deterministic consensus algorithm exists. The result has been mechanically verified, even under fairness assumptions. It does not say agreement can never be reached. It says only that, under the model's assumptions, no algorithm can always reach it in bounded time, and in practice the bad case is highly unlikely. Randomized consensus algorithms circumvent the result by achieving safety and liveness with overwhelming probability, even under worst-case scheduling.
